DEMOCRATIC CONVENTIONS.
Congressman Henderson Nominated at Salisbury-A Judge and Solicitor at Lexington.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
HARLOTTE. N. C., August 1.—The Ju

[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

CHARLOTTE, N. C., August 1.—The Judicial Convention of the Eighth district met at Lexington to-day. The Committee on Resolutions recommended Judge A. S. Merrimon for Chief Justice and Judge Walter Clark for Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of North Carolina. Resolutions were passed heartily endorsing Vance for reelection to the United States Senate.

FOR SOLICITOR AND JUDGE.

B. F. Long was nominated for the office of solicitor by acclamation. The names of R. F. Armfield, of Iredell, and M. S. Robbins, of Randolph, were put in nomination for judge. The contest between the rival contestants was spirited. Armfield, however was nominated by a vote of 162 to 103.

HENDERSON BENOMINATED.

The congressional convention for the Seventh district met in Salisbury to-day. There has been considerable doubt all along as to whether Hon. John S. Henderson, the present incumbent, or Hon. A. L. Leazer, a new candidate, would win the nomination. Henderson was nominated by a vote of 176 to 123. After the result was declared Mr. Leazer made a very strong and patriotic speech, pledging his support to Henderson.

CUT WITH A RAZOR.

To-day while the Town Marshal of Rutherfordton was attempting to arrest a negro named Greely McDowell he came very near being killed. McDowell resisted and tried to cut the Marshal with a razor. The Marshal had to shoot him to protect himself. The wound is serious, but not necessarily fatal.

NEARLY A RACE WAR.

This came near precipitating a race war. A crowd of negroes soon gathered, and the Marshal, who had already emptied all the chambers of his revolver, had to fly for safety. McDowell and his friends swear that they will shoot the officer on sight. Some of the negroes who took a prominent part in the affray have been placed in jail.

THE WEAPONS.
Three negroes were injured severely. Razors and rocks were the offensive weapons of the negroes.

RIOT IN NORTH CAROLINA. Attempt of a Colored Mob to Take a Prisoner Out of the Marshal's Hands.
CHARLOTTE, N. C., Aug. 3.—While the Town Marshal of Rutherfordton was attempting to arrest Greeley McDowell, a negro, yesterday he came very near being killed. McDowell resisted the officer with a razor in one hand and a club in the other. Suddenly a crowd of twenty negroes swarmed around the officer and demanded the release of McDowell, whom he had at last secured. With stones, pistols, and clubs the negroes pursued the officer. One negro came up to the officer and catching hold of McDowell tried to pull him from the officer.

Seeing that he could not keep his prisoner, the Marshal pulled his revolver and began firing into the crowd that was still pressing him. He emptied his revolver and had to run for his life, followed by a howling mob of negroes.

Officer Hardin ran into a store for more ammunition, and for a long while it was teared that the town authorities would have to call upon the State troops to restore peace. The negroes are in a terrible state of excitement, and swear that as soon as they can get a chance at Hardin they will shoot him down. It is learned on reliable authority that the negroes are plotting for a more successful riot in the near future. They say they have been downrodden by the citizens of Rutherfordton: that they have been deprived of their rights under the Constitution, and in the future they will see that privileges are extended to them.

McDowell is badly wounded, and is thought to be in a dangerous condition. Three other negroes received bullet wounds from Officer Hardin's pistol.

Time to Come Home.
A dispatch from Australia says:

"The steamer Lubeck, from Apia, brings rumors of disorders in Samoan villages. In the opinion of the Europeans these disorders point out the necessity of the three treaty powers, England, Germany and the United States forming a proper government for Samoa."

In the opinion of THE CITIZEN—an opinion unquestionably necessary to rightly settle this question—the best thing the United States can do is to make its best bow to Samoa and come home. The moon is of far more interest to us and just a little less dangerous than the land where this particular brand of Pacific Islander stalks around in the full glory of unblushing nakedness and where the German rules regardless of Uncle Sam and the claims of justice.

CUT HIS VICTIM'S HEAD OFF. Remarkable Story Told by a Negro Who Kills a White Man.
LEXINGTON, Ky., Aug. 19.—John Henderson, colored, severed the head off Gilbert Satterwhite, a white man, last night with a razor. Satterwhite was a farmer, and a brother-in-law of James T. Williams, the turfman, who brought out Luke Blackburn, Checkmate, and other horses. His wife and children had gone to visit at Mr. Williams's home in Eminence, Ky., and he hired John Henderson's wife to keep house for him while his wife was gone. He lived twelve miles west of here, and last night he started to Midway, a little town in Woodford county. Henderson's wife asked to go with him, and he gave her a seat in the buggy. That was the last seen of him alive.

About 11 o'clock John Henderson called at the house of Dr. Seely in Midway and told him that he was wounded. The Doctor found he had been shot in the left shoulder, the bullet ranging upward, making a wound not very serious. After much persuasion the negro told the doctor that he was on his way to Mr. Satterwhite's, and that when two miles from Midway he saw Satterwhite and his wife in a compromising position by the roadside. He grappled with Satterwhite, when the latter drew a pistol and shot Henderson as described. This made Henderson wild, and he drew his razor and began cutting his antagonist. After he had carved him in a terrible manner he succeeded in getting his pistol away from him, and with the weapon fired a bullet into Satterwhite's brain. Not satisfied
bile manner he succeeded in getting his pistol away from him, and with the weapon fired a bullet into Satterwhite's brain. Not satisfied with this he grabbed the man by the hair and severed the head from the body.

Then he looked for his wife, but she was not in sight.

When his story was told the Doctor took him to a constable and he was sent to jail. A posse of citizens went to the spot where Henderson said Satterwhite's body had been left, and sure enough there lay the mutilated remains of the young farmer. They were removed to his home and his wife was sent for. The neighbors of the dead man do not believe Henderson's story. They say that because the negro had been discharged from Satterwhite's employ he took advantage of his wife in the buggy to wreak vengeance on his late employer. They think he shot himself in the shoulder for the purpose of upholding his story of self-defence. There is strong talk of lynching him.

LYNCHING A MURDERER. A BRUTAL NEGRO HANGED BY A MOB IN KENTUCKY. FEARS THAT THE BLACKS WILL RETALIATE UPON THE LYNCHERS.
John Henderson, the Slayer of Gilbert Natterwhite, Taken from Jail and Strung Up to a Tree—Henderson's Wife Arrested as an Accomplice in Her Husband's Crime.

LEXINGTON, Ky., Aug. 21. —John Henderson, the negro who killed Gilbert Satterwhite near Midway last Monday night, was lynched near Versailles about 3 o'clock this morning. During a heavy rainstorm the jailer of Woodford County Jail, R. W. Shipp, was awakened by some one calling. He asked what was wanted.

"We have a prisoner from Frankfort and wish to put him in your jail till daylight," was the answer that came out of the darkness.

The jailer sent his deputy, Ed Yogel, downstairs with the keys. When Yogel opened the door he looked into the muzzle of a big pistol. The owner of the pistol said: "We want John Henderson, and you must give us the keys."

The deputy handed them over and about fifteen closely masked men marched into the corridor. They looked for Henderson for several minutes, and one of them remarked: "I don't see him. We will have to make Yogel bring him out."

At that moment Henderson walked out of his cell and, with the most abandoned bravado, exclaimed in a loud voice: "I killed Gil Satterwhite; I 'spose I'm the man you're looking fur."

"Yes," replied the spokesman, "we do want you. Come with us."
The negro went with them uncomplainingly. Outside the jail they were joined by ten or fifteen more masked men. The entire party went out the Frankfort pike about a mile and stopped under a locust tree in front of G. M. Fishback's residence. One man had an inch-and-a-half seaweed rope. This was soon tied around Henderson's neck, and the spokesman said to him:

"You can now pray; we intend to hang you to this tree."

The negro kneeled down. At that moment a flash of lightning illuminated the victim's black features, and he made a most piteous appeal to the Almighty to save his soul. Not one word of confession, however, escaped his thick lips, nor was there any appeal for mercy to the wet and angry men around him.

When he had finished his supplications he arose and in a firm voice said: "I am ready."

"All right," replied the leader of the mob, and willing hands strung the body of Gilbert Satterwhite's slayer in the air.

When his feet were a little more than a foot from the ground the other end of the rope was made taut and the men stepped away. For fifteen minutes the body swayed back and forth, the legs moved up and down, and then all was still.

Two of the men approached the hanging man and after feeling of his pulse pronounced him dead. All then mounted their horses and rode away.

When Mr. Fishback arose at 5 o'clock this morning he saw Henderson's body hanging to his tree. He went to Versailles and notified the Sheriff. The latter went for the Coroner, and that officer held an inquest. The verdict was that Henderson came to his death by hanging at the hands of persons unknown. The body was buried in Versailles at the county's expense.

Gilbert Satterwhite, the victim, was a white man and a farmer. His brother-in-law, James T. Williams, the turfman who brought out Luke Blackburn, Checkmate and other celebrated horses, lives at Eminence. At the time of the killing Mrs. Satterwhite and her children were visiting at Williams's home. Henderson claimed to have found Satterwhite in a compromising position with Mrs. Henderson by the roadside. He confronted them and was shot in the shoulder by Mr. Satterwhite. The negro said this so enraged him that he drew a razor and literally hacked his victim to pieces, completely severing his head from his body.

This story is not believed by the people of the neighborhood, who think Henderson took this method of wreaking vengeance upon the farmer, by whom he had been employed, but who had recently discharged him for misconduct.

Henderson's wife is in jail as an accessory. Several bullet holes were found in the back of Satterwhite's buggy.

The negroes of Versailles and Midway are very much excited over the lynching, and many people fear they will adopt some method of revenge for what they seem to think was the murder of Henderson.

LYNCHED A NEGRO. He Waylaid and Killed a Farmer Who Had Discharged Him From His Service.
MIDWAY, Ky.. Aug. 21.—John Henderson, who murdered Gilbert Satterwhite, a white farmer, near here night before last, was taken from jail about 2 o'clock this morning by a mob and strung up to a tree in the edge of town. He confessed the killing, but he said he did not know why he did it. Henderson's crime was particularly atrocious. He assaulted Mr. Satterwhite while that gentleman was driving along the road after dark, shooting him first and afterward cutting him with a razor. When found, Mr. Satterwhite's head was almost cut from his body, and he had seven other terrible gashes on his body, any one of which would have proved fatal.

The testimony indicates an accessory to the murder, and another negro was arrested to-day. The chances are that he will be hanged to-night. The negroes killed Satterwhite because of their being discharged by him from a threshing machine gang a few weeks ago. The colored people are reported to be greatly incensed at the hanging, and threaten to avenge it on the whites. Trouble is feared.

SENATOR QUAY, who is a thorough politician, if not an able statesman, recognizing that the best sentiment of the country including very many of his own party, is against the enactment of Reed's abominable Force bill, by which the republican party is to retain power by the help of partisan courts and bayonet interference, has succeeded in killing the measure for this session at least. Consequently at the November elections the republicans will not do "their own registration, their own enumeration and their own certification." There was a strong minority in favor of the immediate passage of the bill, but Quay and his followers were in the majority and carried their point to postpone its consideration till next session, agreeing, however, that it may be called up first thing at the December meeting. It is very safe now to predict that it will never be called up. The people will express their condemnation of the outrage at the Congressional elections in such thunder tones that the audacious party in power will be brought to a realization of the fact that its acts of usurpation and its disregard of the constitution, are execrated and despised by such a majority as will not submit to its rough shod effort to blot out the Southern States. Senator Quay may be a very bad man, but the South has reason to thank him for one manly act, for by it the certainty of race conflicts and blood-shed is averted.

RAUM, the pension commissioner, is undergoing investigation of the charge that he is running the office in "cahoot" with Pension Agent Lemon, or what amounts to that. He admits that he "borrowed" $12,000 from him, but it will be hard to convince the world, if he does the whitewashing committee, that the sum was not his share of the booty he is raking from the treasury into Lemon's hands by favorably passing on the many outrageous applications for pension which that shark presents. Mr. Cooper, the congressman who made the charges, was so outraged by the one-sided action of the committee that he refused to serve longer on it, but he finally consented to see the thing out.

WHILE in Lexington Friday night we dropped into the busy office of the Transcript and found Major D. E. Caldwell and his excellent assistant, Mr. C. W. Townsend, and others busily engaged in preparing the matter for the next day's paper. Neither of them is ever too busy to be clever, however, and the major took the time to show us over his office, to which he had recently added a fast Cottrell press, an eight-horse engine and many other appliances necessary to the steady increase of the patronage and popularity of his paper. The Transcript is a paying property and we hope to live to see it make millionaires of both the gentlemen named above.

The woman suffragists seem to have captured the Mississippi constitutional convention. A proposition is before the body to grant the right to vote to women and make an educational-property qualification necessary to the exercise of the bailot. In their zeal to prevent negro supremacy the constitution-makers like drowning men are catching at straws. Rather a thousand times that the most ignorant negro should vote than that our own white women should be brought into the debasing influence that unfortunately surrounds the ballot box.

Hon. BEN S. ROBBINS, late of Oldham county and formerly State Senator of Kentucky, died in Tacoma, Washington, last week. He was at one time a very bright man, but the demon drink got possession of him, wrecking him morally, physically and pecuniarily and at last putting him in a dishonored grave. Young man, look not upon the wine when it is red.

It is said that Mary Anderson Navaro, finding married life a dull and prosy business, will again return to the stage, which she honored by her talents and elevated by her purity of character. There are but few actresses who like her never had the suspicion of a scandal to smirch her fair name.

MIDDLESBORO will entertain the editors of Kentucky on the 11th and 12th of next month and Editor Thomas H. Arnold is now issuing invitations. The big pot is going to be put in the little one and everything done to make the boys have a good time in the Magic City.

WILD speculation and the over-done boom business have produced the natural result of a stringent money market and signs of a panic are portentious. The probability is that those who have not "unloaded" will "hold the bag" to their loss and sorrow.

THERE were three murders and two murderous assaults in Cincinnati Sunday and yet the papers over there sneer at the Dark and Bloody Ground.

The lynching in Woodford was not only an unnecessary but a very reprehensible act. The negro was in custody and as sure of judicial execution as anything could be. There is too much of this kind o business and too few jailers who are worthy to carry the keys of the prisons. The Woodford jailer made no effort to save his prisoner, but admitted the mob with not even a feigned obstruction, evidently being in sympathy with it. There may be times when mob law is justifiable, but in most cases the men who compose the mobs are the worst characters and as much deserving of death as their victims.

EDITOR LEWIS, of the Somerset Republican, is mean enough to remark: "Judge Tinsley, since he has heard from the returns, says Kentucky is democratic beyond a doubt." Yes, the judge is a sadder and we hope a more sensible man than he was. Because the defeated candidate and a few of his friends suiked, he imagined Kentucky democrats were fools enough to permit the best office in the State to go to a republican, but he was mistaken. A majority of 51,000 or more against him would convince any man that "Kentucky is democratic beyond a doubt."

A private letter from Danville says that the refusal of Postmaster Van Pelt to handle the Advocate unless it was folded to suit his fancy was a piece of political spite-work on the part of the official, which we thought him unworthy of. In his statement of the case Editor Woolfolk indulges in no invective and does it apparently so fair that the public will necessarily side with him and against the man, who, if reports be true, acted both autocratically and unaccommodatingly.

THE Senate devoted Saturday to eulogies of Senator James Birney Beck and a number of eloquent ones were delivered, including those of Blackburn, Ingalls, Evarts, Vance, Carlisle, Plumb, Hale and others. The dead statesman was a partisan by nature and never failed to assert it when necessary, but he counted among his fastest friends a majority of the members of the opposite side of the House, who loved him for his honest heart and rugged cordiality.

Hon. GREEN A. DENHAM has again assumed editorial control of the Inter-State News, Messrs. Wm. McCormack and A. J. Seeley, having retired to accept more remunerative positions. Bro. Denham is a good writer and one of the cleverest of men and will no doubt make the paper a power in the land.
